paras: The killing of Booth was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Booth near Satartia, Yazoo County, Mississippi, on Saturday, August 12, 1882, by two white men after he refused to let them ride in his wagon. Both men escaped, and a Jackson dispatch on the shooting ran in papers across the country, several of which headlined it as murder.

According to the Southern Herald of Liberty, Mississippi, Samuel N. Mooney and Jesse Williams asked to ride in Booth's wagon near Satartia, and he refused. The refusal "provoked harsh words," the paper said, "which resulted in the shooting by Mooney." The wire dispatch described both men as having "shot and fatally wounded" Booth, and some headlines reported him killed. Booth's given name and the exact spot and hour of the shooting do not appear in the coverage.
Every account ended with the same line, that both men escaped. No report of an arrest, inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached most readers as a one-sentence telegram datelined Jackson, August 14, which the Dallas Daily Herald identified as a Jackson special relayed from New Orleans. Editors outside the state gave it pointed headlines: the Wheeling Register ran "Negro Murdered," the National Republican in Washington "An Unprovoked Murder," and the Savannah Morning News "A Negro Brutally Murdered." Others used flatter headings, such as "Shot Him" in Dallas, "They Wanted to Ride" in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and "Negro Shot and Killed" in Memphis, or folded the item into crime roundups.

Condensed versions altered the details as the item was copied. The St. Paul Daily Globe and the Morris Tribune dropped Satartia and put the shooting "At Jackson, Miss.," the Jamestown Weekly Alert printed "Jackson, Mich." and "Mordy," and a news summary in the Daily Gazette and Daily Republican named the second man Richardson. The Benton Weekly Record ran it as late as August 31 under the heading "Killed a Negro" with a garbled "Jacksonville, Miss., Aug. 24" dateline.

In Mississippi, the Southern Herald and the Brookhaven Ledger printed the fuller version, with both men's full names, as brief state news without comment. Only the Brookhaven Ledger named Yazoo County, and only the Southern Herald identified Mooney as the man who fired.

The wire dispatch and both Mississippi papers named the second man Williams, while one widely copied summary called him Richardson. Most papers said the two men shot Booth together, but the Southern Herald attributed the shot to Mooney alone.

bases: Two white men, not officers and not described as a mob or band, shot a Black man who refused them a ride in his wagon (A7, A15, A20).

A Jackson wire dispatch carried by many papers (A5, A7, A10) and two Mississippi weeklies with fuller names (A15, A20) agree on the victim, the wagon refusal, the fatal shooting and the escape, though the weeklies may draw on the same source.
